```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(datasauRus)
```

# Exercise 1

A data frame with 1846 rows and 3 variables(rows):

- dataset: indicates which dataset the data are from

- x: x-values

- y: y-values

# Exercise 2

```{r ex-2}
dino_data <- datasaurus_dozen |>
  filter(dataset == "dino")
ggplot(data = dino_data, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()
dino_data |>
  summarize(r = cor(x, y))
```

# Exercise 3

```{r ex-3}
star_data <- datasaurus_dozen |>
  filter(dataset == "star")
ggplot(data = star_data, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()
star_data |>
  summarize(r = cor(x, y))
```

> Based on the plot, I expect a close to zero correlation. The values are all over the place and they don't follow a singular pattern.

> The two r values are almost the same.

# Exercise 4

```{r ex-4}
slant_up_data <- datasaurus_dozen |>
  filter(dataset == "slant_up")
ggplot(data = slant_up_data, mapping = aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point()
slant_up_data |>
  summarize(r = cor(x, y))


```

> The plotted dataset looks like a series of parallel lines. Since the plots seem to be slanting up, I expect a positive correlation.

> The coefficient is close to zero. The value is less than zero, therefore less than what I expected. The correlation captures that there is a negative linear relationship between the variables, but does not describe the scattered nature of the dataset. And therefore we cannot infer anything of value only based on the correlation.

# Exercise 5

```{r ex-5}
ggplot(datasaurus_dozen, aes(x = x, y = y, color = dataset))+
  geom_point()+
  facet_wrap(~ dataset, ncol = 3) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
datasaurus_dozen |>
  group_by(dataset) |>
  summarize(r = cor(x, y))

```

> None of the correlations are significant enough; they're close to zero. We can understand that we cannot enforce linear relationships on datasets.
